tool.name: CombineHabitatFactors
tool.summary: Combines habitat factor rasters that are ALREADY scored on the 0-100 suitability scale into one habitat suitability model, by weighted geometric mean (recommended: a 0 score in any factor zeroes the cell -- Liebig's Law of the Minimum) or weighted additive mean (equivalent to Esri's Weighted Overlay), with weights summing to 100. The companion to Create Habitat Suitability Model: that tool can save its reclassified factors exactly so this one can re-combine them under different weights or methods without repeating the reclassification. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Combine Habitat Factors tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHAT THIS TOOL DOES, AND WHEN TO REACH FOR IT. This is the second half of Create Habitat Suitability Model, split out on its own: it performs the weighted combine but SKIPS the remap step, taking factors whose cells are already 0-100 suitability scores. Its main purpose is experimentation. Building a habitat model is iterative -- weights are expert judgment, not measured quantities, and the workshop book is frank that weighting is one of the weakest parts of these models -- so you will want to try land cover at 60 then at 70, or compare geometric against additive, several times over. Run Create Habitat Suitability Model once with "Save reclassified habitat factors" checked, then re-combine the saved _r rasters here as many times as you like; only the cheap combine step is repeated. It equally accepts 0-100 factors scored by any other means (a Normalize Existing HSM output, a surface you reclassified yourself).
THE MATH, IDENTICAL TO THE ORIGINAL. Weights are checked to sum to exactly 100 and normalized to w/100. The GEOMETRIC mean raises each factor's score to its normalized weight and multiplies the results: a 0 in ANY factor makes the cell 0 no matter how good the others are -- Liebig's Law of the Minimum, the workshop book's recommended default (section 2.4), because habitat suitability probably is limited by the worst factor. The ADDITIVE mean multiplies each score by its normalized weight and sums -- Esri's Weighted Overlay -- letting strong factors compensate for weak ones. Either way the result stays on 0-100, and the 0-100 scale keeps its biological anchor points (100 = best habitat, 80 = lowest score typically associated with successful breeding, 60 = lowest for consistent use and breeding, 30 = occasional non-breeding use, 0 = absolute non-habitat; workshop book section 2.3).
INPUTS ARE EXPECTED ON 0-100, AND THE TOOL CHECKS. A factor with cells outside 0-100 draws a warning with the count -- the combine runs anyway, but an out-of-range input usually means a raw (un-reclassified) raster was supplied by mistake; that belongs in Create Habitat Suitability Model instead. Under the geometric mean, NEGATIVE cells have no defined fractional power and become NoData, with a warning.
THE FIRST FACTOR DEFINES THE OUTPUT GRID. The output takes its cell size, extent, and coordinate system from the first factor; any factor on a different grid is resampled onto it (nearest neighbour) with a message. Cells that are NoData in ANY factor are NoData in the output. Any number of factors is accepted (the original capped at six).
EVERY OUTPUT KNOWS ITS PLACE IN THE CHAIN. The output is stamped with a machine-readable record naming every factor and weight and the combining method, so the Corridor Analysis Data Report and the downstream corridor tools can trace exactly how the model was built.
ENVIRONMENTS. This tool is grid-native: the analysis runs on, and the output is delivered on, the input raster's own grid and coordinate system. The Output Coordinate System, Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Mask environment settings are deliberately NOT applied -- honoring them would re-project, crop, or resample a finished analysis whose statistics and metadata describe the original grid. To get the result in another coordinate system, project the finished output with Project Raster as a deliberate step. The scratch workspace and overwrite-output settings are honored.
CREDITS AND REFERENCES. The original CorridorDesigner HSM tools are by Dan Majka (dan@corridordesign.org, 2006-2007); these ArcGIS Pro versions are by Jeff Jenness and Dan Majka. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

param.name: factors
param.displayname: Reclassified habitat factors (raster, weight; weights must sum to 100)

dialogReference.para: One row per factor: a raster already scored on the 0-100 suitability scale (typically the _r rasters saved by Create Habitat Suitability Model), and its weight. Any number of rows; weights must be positive and sum to exactly 100. The FIRST row defines the output grid; others are resampled onto it (nearest neighbour) with a message. Cells outside 0-100 draw a warning -- usually the sign a raw, un-reclassified raster was picked by mistake.

Geometric Mean (the default and the workshop book's recommendation) multiplies each factor's score raised to its normalized weight: a 0 in ANY factor zeroes the cell -- Liebig's Law of the Minimum. Additive Mean sums score times normalized weight (equivalent to Esri's Weighted Overlay): deficiencies in one factor CAN be averaged away by the others. Both keep the result on 0-100.

The combined habitat suitability model, on the 0-100 scale with 100 = best habitat. A path in a folder without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF. The output carries full statistics plus metadata recording every factor, weight, and the combining method.

scriptExample.title: Combine Habitat Factors example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Re-combines the reclassified factors saved by Create Habitat Suitability Model under a different weighting, then once more with the additive mean for comparison.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# method options: "Geometric Mean" (recommended), "Additive Mean" arcpy.jenness.CombineHabitatFactors( [[r"C:\project\hsm\landcover_r.tif", 70], [r"C:\project\hsm\elevation_r.tif", 15], [r"C:\project\hsm\dist_roads_r.tif", 15]], "Geometric Mean", r"C:\project\hsm\Badger_HSM_w70.tif")
arcpy.jenness.CombineHabitatFactors( [[r"C:\project\hsm\landcover_r.tif", 70], [r"C:\project\hsm\elevation_r.tif", 15], [r"C:\project\hsm\dist_roads_r.tif", 15]], "Additive Mean", r"C:\project\hsm\Badger_HSM_w70_add.tif")
